PAPER: Artificial Intelligence Review (2026) 59:32 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11430-4 A survey on deep learning for 2D and 3D human pose estimation Marsha Mariya Kappan1 · Eduardo Benitez Sandoval2 · Erik Meijering1 · Francisco Cruz1,3 Received: 1 August 2025 / Accepted: 19 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Human pose estimation is a fundamental task in computer vision and robotics that in- volves detecting the human body joints from images or videos. It became a rapidly evolv- ing field with applications ranging from action recognition to healthcare. This survey provides a detailed review of various methods in 2D and 3D human pose estimation for single-person and multi-person contexts in both image-based and video-based scenarios. We present a comprehensive categorization and comparison of available 2D and 3D pose datasets with an emphasis on their strengths and limitations. In addition, we also provide an overview of various evaluation metrics and loss functions commonly used to evalu- ate the accuracy and robustness of pose estimation models. We further discuss emerging trends, offering readers an insight into current trends in the field. We then explore key application domains where pose estimation plays an important role. The survey explains in detail about challenges in human pose estimation, including occlusion, data scarcity, pri- vacy concerns, generalization issues, and model complexity, and suggests potential future research directions. Overall, this review aims to guide researchers in understanding current methods, datasets, and applications, while pointing out open issues and highlighting the future scope of human pose estimation. Keywords Human pose estimation · Deep learning · 2D pose estimation · 3D pose estimation · Pose estimation survey 1 Introduction Human pose estimation (HPE) is an evolving field in computer vision that aims to identify and locate different human body joints, also known as keypoints, from visual data such as images or videos. HPE has applications in a wide range of areas (e.g., activity moni- toring (Amiri et al. 2014; Gu et al. 2021), human robot interaction (Martini et al. 2024), gaming (Abe et al. 2024), camera surveillance (Cao and Yan 2024; Zhu et al. 2024)). M. Kappan et al. systems. As research progresses, HPE is evolving from simply detecting individual poses to understanding and tracking how people move over time. This development highlights the increasing need for systems that can capture complex real-time human movements for real- world applications. HPE systems that integrate spatiotemporal context help HPE systems to identify and track human motions over time, which results in a more precise understand- ing (Feng et al. 2023; Xi et al. 2024). Traditional methods, which utilize edge detection (Jabri et al. 2000) and silhouette anal- ysis (Haritaoglu et al. 1998), were among some of the early methods for estimating the poses. But they were limited by their inability to estimate complex poses and poses under occlusions. The key turning point in the evolution of pose estimation was the introduction of models such as Active Shape Model (ASM) (Cootes et al. 1995) and Active Appearance Model (AAM) (Cootes et al. 1998). ASM, which uses Principal Component analysis (PCA), locates variations in shape by statistical modeling, while AAM goes a step further, integrat- ing both shape and texture variations. These models laid the foundations for modern HPE methods such as feature extraction and statistical learning. The emergence of deep learning created a breakthrough in pose estimation. Deep- Pose (Toshev and Szegedy 2014a) framework proposed by Toshev and Szegedy played an important role in showing the power of deep learning in HPE. They approached pose estimation as a regression problem to directly predict the positions of keypoints from input images, then used deep networks to predict human keypoint locations. This was followed by heatmap-based approaches in which deep networks generate probability maps, which are 2D Gaussian distributions representing the probability of presence of each joint at particular locations in the map (Cao et al. 2017; Cai et al. 2020). 1.1 Previous surveys and motivation Many surveys focusing on HPE have been published in recent years. Distinguishing between 2D and 3D HPE is important as both represent different challenges and aspects of the HPE problem. 2D methods focus on joint locations in image space, which is simpler and sufficient for basic tasks. However, they are insufficient for tasks that require spatial depth and body orientation, which are critical in understanding motion patterns in real-world scenarios. In contrast, 3D HPE helps to focus on joint positions in three-dimen- sional space, which makes it more complex but also crucial for application in real-world scenarios. Considering these, this review considers 2D and 3D HPE methods separately but as interconnected areas. We provide a detailed analysis of previous works employing deep learning methods for 2D and 3D HPE. We discuss the strengths and limitations of HPE and offer a compari- son of different approaches. We classify different methods based on the number of people involved–a single person or a group of people– and further differentiate based on whether the input is an image or a video. This article not only discusses various datasets but also pro- vides an overview of applications and their role in benchmark performance in various meth- ods. By highlighting the emerging methods and major challenges in HPE, this survey aims to provide a complete overview of HPE and to emphasize opportunities for future research directions in the field of HPE. Each person is represented using 17 keypoints in this dataset. Each annotation in this dataset includes the image file name, width, and height of the image, the object class, bounding box coordinates, segmentation mask, keypoint coordi- nates, and five captions that describe each scene. It consists of a wide range of activities such as daily activities, crowded scenarios, and complex interactions among people. Researchers use this for benchmarking because of its diversity. The authors of COCO introduced Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS) that extends Intersection over Union (IoU), which became a standard metric for multi-person benchmarking. Although it has diverse data, it also has imbalances in certain activities. For example, public and outdoor environments are heav- ily represented, whereas indoor and industrial contexts are comparatively less represented. 2.1.6 PoseTrack This dataset is a video-based multi-person tracking dataset. Occlusion flags were also assigned for all the joints. PoseTrack18 (Andriluka et al. 2018) expanded the dataset with 550 video sequences with 66,374 frames using 15 body joints. Later in 2021, PoseTrack21 (Doering et al. 2022) was introduced by re-annotating the videos from PoseTrack18 (Andriluka et al. 2018). It includes different varieties of everyday actions, including indoor and outdoor activities. However, it contains 2D video sequences only. Most of the existing datasets work well in normal scenarios when there is proper lighting, but their failure rate is high in extreme scenarios. EHPT-XC used a triplet camera system, which consists of an RGB camera and a pair of event cameras, which helps to capture scenes with poor lighting or motion blur. The dataset includes a balanced amount of data for low-lit or well-lit and indoor or outdoor scenarios. It consists of 16K images with 38K annotated poses. The inte- gration of an event camera allows the research to step into event-guided HPE, which helps in capturing fast motions and uneven illumination conditions. However, the data is 2D and there is no 3D information, which makes it unsuitable for 3D applications. The size of the dataset is also relatively small compared to other large-scale datasets. Fig. 6 Different human body models. a skeletal model, b planar model, c kinematic model, d volumetric model 3.1 Skeletal model This is the most common model used to represent a human body (Li et al. 2020; Geng et al. 2021). A human body is considered a structured skeletal system of joints (shoulders, elbows, etc.) connected with lines that represent limbs. The number of joints varies from one representation to another (17 for COCO and 16 for MPII). This is widely used in both 2D and 3D HPE. This set of joints with interconnected limbs forms a graph-like structure. However, this representation has limitations in modeling complex human motions as it does not consider the motion constraints of joints or rotational constraints. 3.2 Planar model The planar model, also known as the contour-based model, represents the shape and appear- ance of the human body using mathematical figures such as rectangles and circles. Ju et al. (1996) proposed a cardboard person model for human tracking where each part of the body is represented using rectangles connected at joint locations. Then the motion is represented using an eight-parameter motion model. However, these representations provide only a rough and simple representation of the human body, lacking the real shape and fine details. Later, Freifeld et al. (2010) proposed a 2D contour person model that represents detailed body contours. This depicts the natural shape of the human body and represents how this shape varies across each individual. 3.3 Kinematic model In the kinematic model, the human body is represented using connected joints with kine- matic constraints. Mehta et al. (2017b) used a kinematic skeleton fitting for real-time 3D HPE. They computed bone length maps, which help to ensure the stability of the skeleton and to guide the prediction. During the kinematic skeleton fitting stage, they replaced the bone lengths of the predicted 3D pose with the fixed bone lengths of a predefined skeleton. This re-targeting guarantees that the bone length is consistent across frames. Kinematic models have gained great attention in 3D HPE in recent years. The model uses normal- izing flows to model complex kinematic priors, enabling more accurate pose reconstruction. It uses a multi-level supervision strategy for loss calculation, which combines fully supervised loss for datasets with 3D annotations, weakly supervised losses applied to datasets with 2D annotations, and self-supervised losses. Unlike traditional methods which predict body joint positions by regression or through heatmap prediction, diffusion-based frameworks follow an iterative denoising pro- cess to obtain correct poses. In this process, they start with random noise, allowing them to better represent uncertainties in 2D-to-3D lifting where multiple pose configurations may exist. Due to their probabilistic nature, they achieve higher accuracy than other determinis- tic models and also achieve better accuracy in challenging real-world scenarios. Li and Lee (2019) proposed one of the early probabilistic methods to use Mixture Den- sity Networks (MDNs) to model pose hypotheses. They considered 2D-to-3D lifting as a multi-modal problem because a single 2D pose can correspond to various 3D poses due to depth ambiguity. They model the posterior distribution as Gaussian mixtures, where the means of Gaussian kernels represent the candidate 3D poses while the variance captures the uncertainties of each hypothesis. A major limitation is that the number of hypotheses must be determined in advance (Holmquist and Wandt 2023). In contrast, Sharma et al. (2019) proposed a method based on Conditional Variational Autoencoders (CVAEs) that aims to produce diverse 3D pose samples on observed 2D keypoints. Their MultiPoseNet generates a diverse set of candidate poses by sampling from a latent distribution to address the ambi- guities. They used ordinal rankings to rank samples that are more consistent with human body structure and aggregate them to generate a 3D pose. However, it requires a relatively complex architecture and lacks diversity in generated hypotheses, since 2D heatmaps are oversimplified, which leads to similar poses even under high uncertainty. To address these issues, Holmquist and Wandt (2023) introduced DiffPose, a conditional diffusion model for generating multiple 3D pose predictions from a single 2D input. Instead of oversimplifying 2D heatmaps, they aim to generate accurate 3D poses that approximate the full posterior distribution. Their method is inspired by Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) (Ho et al. 2020) because of their training stability and ability to generate diverse predictions. However, DiffPose remains computationally heavy and has latency due to thousands of denoising steps at inference. D3DP (Shan et al. 2023) is another diffusion- based model that also predicts multiple 3D candidate poses. Unlike DiffPose (Holmquist and Wandt 2023), which relies on pose-level averaging, D3DP (Shan et al. 2023) introduces a novel aggregation method, which is Joint-level Pose Multiple Aggregation (JPMA) that aggregates at the joint level, leading to more accurate predictions. It enhances the robust- ness of their method through strong augmentation strategies. D3DP also uses Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) (Song et al. 2022) during inference, which allows it to reduce the number of denoising steps, thereby making the model more efficient while main- taining accuracy. For spatio-temporal reasoning, it uses MixSTE (Zhang et al. 2022a), a transformer-based backbone known for its ability to capture spatial and temporal dependen- cies well. In this section, we discuss the challenges and future research directions of HPE. 9.1 Occlusion and biomechanical constraints Accurate localization of human body joints is one of the major challenges in HPE. Occlu- sion occurs when parts of the human body become hidden behind objects or persons. It can be self-occlusion, which is due to overlapping limbs, or person/object occlusion, which may be due to interference in crowded scenes or external objects that partially hide some parts of the body. Occlusions can be static or dynamic. Static occlusions occur when a person is partially hidden by a stationary object, and in contrast, dynamic occlusions can be caused by moving objects or people. Scenarios with poor lighting conditions or extreme camera angles can make body parts invisible or partially hidden. Since most deep learning models rely on visual cues, when these are missing, the performance of the HPE model may drop significantly. Although some methods have been proposed to deal with this issue (Wang et al. 2025; Bai et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2022), robust handling of occlusion still remains an open challenge. In video-based HPE, dynamic occlusions disrupt the temporal consistency, which in turn lowers tracking accuracy. Some methods leverage temporal consistency to recover occluded poses over time (Pavllo et al. 2019). However, in prolonged occlusions, the ability to depend on nearby visual cues and motion sequences from previous frames becomes less effective. Future research directions could explore gray-box approaches which fuse biomechanics and kinematics with learned pose priors, enabling models to predict physically plausible poses during prolonged occlusions. Purely data-driven HPE methods often struggle when multiple body joints are occluded or during longer occlusions, as they lack sufficient visual informa- tion. Instead of depending on visual cues, future HPE systems could incorporate various biomechanical constraints of human movements, such as limb length limits, symmetry of the human body, joint angle limits, and kinematic chain rules, into the prediction process. When visual information about a joint is missing, a method that depends purely on visual information may yield anatomically implausible predictions. In such scenarios, biomechan- ics provides kinematic information that allows the model to recognize how the body can or cannot move based on the available visual information and biomechanics. Traditionally, MoCap-based systems have been the benchmark for obtaining biomechan- ically accurate human poses. These systems use multiple calibrated cameras to track the reflective markers placed on the human body and are often captured in controlled laboratory environments. The resulting trajectories are then processed with biomechanical optimiza- tion tools like OpenSim (Delp et al. 2007) to obtain accurate kinematic data. However, this 1 3 A survey on deep learning for 2D and 3D human pose estimation Page 51 of 68 32 is costly and time-consuming and impractical for deployment in large-scale non-laboratory environments. Recent advances in monocular HPE have shifted towards using parametric body models like SMPL. While these models enhance pose predictions, their simplified representations lack biomechanical accuracy, which limits their applicability in areas such as healthcare, sports, and ergonomics. So, future research directions should shift towards integrating pose priors with biomechanics, which can generate anatomically plausible poses under occlusion, even though some joints are occluded. In parallel, multi-modal informa- tion such as inertial sensors and depth information, or acoustic signals, can provide valuable information when vision alone is insufficient, facilitating robust, biomechanically accurate HPE methods. 9.2 Data scarcity Deep learning based HPE methods heavily rely on large amounts of data for effective train- ing. Creating high-quality data with accurate annotations requires expensive setups and labeling costs. While 2D datasets provide millions of images, available 3D datasets are scarce. The collection of high-quality 3D pose data is expensive and difficult, especially in wild scenarios. As a result, most of the existing 3D datasets are collected in a controlled indoor laboratory environment and are limited in diversity. A promising direction to over- come this is to use synthetic data, which researchers have already started exploring. The use of simulation environments for creating large-scale, diverse 3D pose datasets in an efficient and quick manner presents a promising research direction. Recent synthetic pose datasets like SynBody (Yang et al. 2023b) highlight the potential and future scope of synthetic data. Another promising future direction is the creation of digital twins, which are virtual humans that obey fundamental laws of physics and biomechanics of human motion to rep- licate characteristics of real individuals. Unlike conventional synthetic datasets that mainly focus on parametric models like SMPL, these models focus mainly on anatomically pre- cise representations and movements of the human body, and person-specific attributes like height, weight, and body proportions. These models can incorporate additional data such as ground reaction forces and muscle activations, along with body keypoints and trajecto- ries. Furthermore, a promising direction is the development of a multi-modal dataset that combines multiple modalities, such as RGB, depth, motion cues, and sensor data, which will help HPE systems to learn diverse cross-model representations and improve robustness under noisy scenarios. Digital twins and multi-modal datasets provide a direction towards diverse and physically valid training data that can significantly advance the robustness of future HPE systems. 9.3 Privacy concerns in HPE HPE plays a major role in many applications; however, application of HPE in sensitive domains such as healthcare, rehabilitation, and monitoring of workspaces, raises concerns about individual’s privacy. Most of the HPE methods rely on images or videos, which may lead to the recording of sensitive personal information alongside pose data. Manual annota- tion of collected pose data includes human annotators, which may lead to an increased risk of data leakage. Many datasets are annotated using third-party services, where data can be transmitted through networks that are not secure. Traditional methods to enhance privacy 1 3 32 Page 52 of 68 M. M. Kappan et al. resulted in the integration of costly sensors or additional data. So, finding a balance between privacy and high performance is challenging. Some methods used anonymization techniques such as removing or blurring facial features to minimize identifiable information. However, over-anonymization can lead to degradation of pose accuracy. Huang et al. (2025a) pro- posed a privacy-enhancing HPE framework that masks sensitive personal information (SPI) like identity of the person using conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs). They also implemented a recovery module, which allows recovery of sensitive personal informa- tion, allowing recovery only by authorized personnel. Their approach achieved 10% higher AP compared to baselines, which is only finetuned on anonymised data. Another method by Sivangi et al. (2025) implements a Projected Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (PDP-SGD), which offers privacy by injecting noise into gradients and projecting them into a low-dimensional subspace, thereby reducing utility loss. While these methods provide valuable insights, they are constrained to 2D settings, and they overlook broader challenges of scalability and fairness, and use heavy architectures that hinder deployment on edge devices. Moreover, domain-specific privacy strategies are important. For instance, in the health- care domain, HPE models could be developed to preserve/monitor clinically relevant, mean- ingful data such as kinematic details while excluding SPI like facial identities. Developing application-specific privacy preservation methods that selectively maintain or remove cer- tain features may ensure privacy without compromising performance. Future work should aim to develop end-to-end privacy-preserving pipelines that address the entire HPE process, from developing secure training strategies to developing lightweight models for deployment on edge devices. In addition to privacy, broader ethical considerations should also be addressed. Bias is a critical issue caused by unbalanced datasets, which may lead to reduced performance across various demographic groups. When a certain group is overrepresented in training data, models trained on it may perform poorly on underrepresented populations. In the con- text of surveillance, this is critical as HPE systems work well for overrepresented popula- tions. This may lead to social inequalities, highlighting the need for fair training strategies. Surveillance technologies ranging from CCTV cameras to drones can improve safety to a great extent, but also raise serious concerns about individual’s privacy and misuse of data. Wheatley (2024) discusses the ethics of surveillance technologies in her article. emphasiz- ing the need to balance privacy and ethics in this digital era and the need of strong policies and clear regulations. Both legal and technological strategies are important to maintain a balance between surveillance and privacy. Legally, many countries have introduced various policies in managing surveillance to protect the rights of individuals. From a technological perspective, methods including encryption, anonymization, and privacy-preserving biomet- rics shows that security can be strengthened. 9.4 Generalization across various domains Generalization capability of a model refers to its ability to perform well when applied to data that are outside of its training distribution. Most of the HPE models are trained on data- sets that include data from specific domains or specific scenarios. However, these models may fail to generalize to unseen scenarios with different camera viewpoints. Models trained on datasets like COCO or Human3.6M may not perform well in industrial or healthcare 1 3 A survey on deep learning for 2D and 3D human pose estimation Page 53 of 68 32 environments due to domain shift. Models trained using data representing people in spe- cific age groups or ethnicities may perform poorly on unrepresented groups of people. Data scarcity in some domains, such as elderly healthcare monitoring, limits the generalization capabilities of the model. Lack of generalization affects the performance of HPE methods in various scenarios. To improve the generalization capability of the model, domain adaptation (Gholami et al. 2022) and self-supervised methods (Wandt and Rosenhahn 2019; Lai et al. 2023) can be integrated. However, they depend on large datasets and do not fully eliminate demographic bias. Likewise, transfer learning approaches that involve fine-tuning the models trained on large datasets using domain-specific data may help models to adapt to diverse conditions Taketsugu and Ukita (2024). To deal with the challenges of maintaining diverse datas- ets across different domains, which can be time-consuming and labor-intensive, Du et al. (2025) proposed a meta-transfer learning approach that uses multi-modal data such as high- frequency surface electromyography (sEMG), visual-inertial odometry (VIO), and image data, which remain computationally intensive and underexplored at scale. Additionally, data augmentation techniques such as altering lighting, modifying poses, and dropping some keypoints improve generalization. To consistently detect body postures regardless of cam- era angles or viewpoints, view-invariant representations can help. By combining these, HPE systems may improve generalization capabilities. To move forward, future research direc- tions should consider developing view-invariant and anthropometry-aware representations that maintain consistency of poses across various viewpoints and diverse body shapes. In addition to these advancements to algorithms and architectures, systematic benchmarking for fairness and generalization is essential. Current evaluations focus on individual datasets, which are limited to particular domains or demographic groups (different ages, genders, eth- nicities, body shapes). The future benchmarks should include fairness across demographies and consider cross-dataset generalization during evaluation. 9.5 Real-time and low-power device deployment Computationally efficient and accurate HPE models are essential in real-time systems such as robotics, augmented/virtual reality (AR/VR), and surveillance systems. The SOTA meth- ods, such as HRNet (Wang et al. 2021a), Hourglass (Newell et al. 2016), and transformer- based methods, have complex architectures that demand high processing power. These models are optimized for accuracy rather than efficiency, which in turn makes them imprac- tical for low-power devices. However, many of the current SOTA HPE systems with high accuracy are computationally heavy. This is a major crisis for the deployment of such mod- els in resource-constrained environments. Lightweight models for HPE is a crucial research direction. Various lightweight mod- els have been proposed (Kappan et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024b), but they often have limited accuracy or limited adaptability in various scenarios. HPE is used in various applications such as healthcare and surveillance, which demand low latency. However, heavy models have high inference time, which leads to delays or inconsistent pose tracking. This may lead to serious concerns in safety-critical applications. Along with the progress in methods and algorithms, advances in hardware have been equally important in enabling real-time HPE. Mostly, HPE methods are designed in a general way that predicts all the joints of the human body. Designing models based on applications may help to avoid unnecessary com- plexity. But in reality, for specific applications, they need only particular joints and not all the body joints equally. In aged care centers, walking patterns and posture will be the prime focus of HPE systems. So, joints like hips, shoulders, and knees are most important. In this case, the tracking of the fingers does not matter much. And in driver monitoring systems, tracking of upper body movements and eye gaze are important. But in contrast, in applica- tions such as sign language detection, even small finger movements are crucial and need to be tracked. Future research should therefore focus on application-aware model design where methods are meant to focus on specific joints or patterns relevant for that domain, thereby avoiding unnecessary model complexities. 9.6 Robustness in challenging real-world scenarios Deploying HPE systems in the real world is often challenging as it degrades pose accuracy due to crowded scenes, motion blur, and low light conditions. In top-down methods, errors are generally from the person detector, which misses identifying bounding boxes around a person when bodies overlap heavily. As bottom-up methods first detect keypoints and then group them, they face difficulties in accurately grouping the detected keypoints in crowded scenes. PoseTrack (Andriluka et al. 2018) highlights several challenges of pose tracking in crowded scenarios. Common challenges include sports scenarios in which individuals per- form rapid movements and complex poses. In team activities, the close proximity of mul- tiple people may confuse pose trackers, leading to identity switches or misclassifications. To address challenges in crowded scenarios, early work by Li et al. (2019) proposed CrowdPose, a Joint-Candidate Single Person Pose Estimator (JC SPPE) method that pre- dicts multiple peak heatmaps for each joint location, which allows it to capture both tar- 1 3 A survey on deep learning for 2D and 3D human pose estimation Page 55 of 68 32 get joints (joints that belong to the person in the bounding box) and joints belonging to nearby people. Then, a joint association algorithm is applied to them, and a person-joint graph is created as a result. This approach improved pose estimation accuracy in crowded scenarios and also generalized well to benchmarks such as COCO (Lin et al. 2015). Build- ing on such foundations, recent approaches have started focusing on temporal cues in vid- eos, where crowded scenarios make person re-identification more challenging. Doering and Gall (2023) introduced a method that uses a gated attention transformer that adapts pose similarity and appearance features using a gating mechanism. To measure similarities between detections, they introduced appearance-based embeddings and along with edge embeddings that encode pose similarities from keypoints. Since pose similarities often fail under rapid motion, they proposed a gated attention transformer that combines appearance features (which help to recover identities after rapid motion) with pose-based cues. While these methods obtain promising results, they are computationally heavy, which limits their application in various real-time applications and edge devices. A potential direction is to use lightweight models such as graph networks or emerging methods based on state-space models (Gu and Dao 2023) to balance both accuracy and computation. Another common challenge in real-world settings is motion-blur and low-light con- dition, which degrades the performance of HPE systems. Zhao et al. (2023) introduced Human from Blur (HfB), a method that jointly performs image deblurring and pose esti- mation. Instead of first enhancing the blurred image and then estimating the pose, they directly recover the person’s pose from the blurred frame. Their method uses pose priors and motion constraints to make the predictions more realistic and applies an adversarial prior to recognize wrong motions. Methods trained on datasets with well-lit data degrade their performance in low-light scenarios. Lee et al. (2023) introduced the ExLPose dataset, the first large-scale benchmark specifically designed for extremely low-light conditions, where even humans struggle to perceive visual content. Traditional methods, which depend on histogram equalization, are heavily used to solve this issue. However these methods are computationally heavy. Instead they proposed a teacher–student framework based on Learn- ing Using Privileged Information (LUPI) combined with lighting-condition-specific batch normalization (LSBN). Unlike earlier datasets such as ExDark (Loh and Chan 2019), which focus on low-light scenarios for other tasks like object detection, EXLPose provides both low-light and well-lit scenarios, offering a more balanced dataset to evaluate the robustness of pose estimation under varying illumination. Ai et al. (2025) proposed a method using two complementary teacher networks without the need of low-light ground-truth data. They addressed the prob- lem of low-light conditions by transferring knowledge from well-lit data, and applying aug- mentations to simulate low-light conditions. Their dual-teacher learning approach consists of a main teacher who is good at detecting poses of visible people and a complementary teacher who detects partially visible people. Despite the advances, this method is con- strained by the quality of pseudo labels and augmentations. Future work could explore diffu- sion models to generate realistic low illumination conditions. Overall, achieving robustness in real-world scenarios remains an open challenge in HPE. Current trends try to address individual issues at a time, either motion blur or low-light conditions. A major trend in HPE is focused on achieving high accuracy by designing deeper and complex architectures. To better illustrate these, Table 7 provides a comparison of different models. Approaches such as HRNet (Wang et al. 2021a) and its vari- ants, and transformer-based approaches like TokenPose(Li et al. 2021), HRFormer (Yuan et al. 2021), and MixSTE (Zhang et al. 2022a) have shown remarkable achievements in pose estimation. However, despite their advancements, these methods face challenges related to high computational requirements and latency, limiting their deployment on resource-con- strained platforms. Diffusion-based methods have recently emerged as a powerful method in pose estimation by improving pose estimation accuracy. These methods treat pose estima- tion as an iterative denoising process, unlike conventional regression methods that directly predicts keypoints. Approaches like D3DP (Shan et al. 2023) and DiffPose (Gong et al. 2023) integrate spatio-temporal transformers with conditional diffusion to improve pose estimation accuracy. However, diffusion models are computationally expensive due to tens to hundreds of iterative denoising steps at inference. Although in HPE systems, accuracy has been the primary focus traditionally, its real- world deployment is constrained by various factors like processing power, memory, and latency. These limitations have led to the need for lightweight architectures to balance effi- ciency and accuracy. More recently, architectures have emerged to address specific chal- lenges. Hourglass Tokenizer (HoT) introduced a Token Pruning Cluster (TPC) to discard redundant frame tokens and a Token Recovering Attention (TRA) to recover spatio-tem- poral information. The pruning happens in deeper layers, and the initial layers still process all tokens. It can be added to existing pose transformers without many modifications. The method achieves good accuracy while cutting off FLOPs (floating point operations) by 50%. Many light-weight variants such as Lite-HRNet (Yu et al. 2021), TokenPose-S (Li et al. 2021), LAP (Kappan et al. 2024), etc. have emerged, which integrate efficient self-attention, depthwise separable convolution, etc to make the model lighter. These models shift from heavy models to optimized architectures, enhancing the speed and power efficiency in real- world HPE systems. Compared with state-of-the-art transformer-based architectures, light- weight HPE models generally achieve lower accuracy. A further challenge is scalability. In top-down multi-person HPE, which requires separate person detection and joint prediction, computation may scale up linearly with the increase in the number of people. Conversely, bottom-up methods, which are more efficient, still face difficulties in joint grouping when the scene is more crowded. Various transformer-based methods have shown great representational power, however their scalability is limited by the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. For increasingly larger crowds, such methods become harder to deploy, especially when available resources are limited. Lightweight models such as LiteHRNet (Yu et al. 2021) and LAP (Kappan et al. 2024) use efficient light-weighting strategies to help improve scalability; however, they often struggle to achieve good pose estimation results due to their limited representational power. Also, most HPE methods operate on fixed computational budgets regardless of the environment on which they are deployed. Kappan et al. 10 Conclusion As shown in this survey, deep learning-based methods for both 2D and 3D human pose estimation, and its application in various fields are a research subject of widespread interest. We systematically categorize 2D and 3D HPE methods for single-person and multi-person scenarios in both images and videos. Each category was further classified into subcategories based on the main idea, key design principles, and supervision strategies. To guide the read- ers through key contributions and evolutions in HPE, we proposed a taxonomy that catego- rizes them across multiple dimensions, including publication year, method vs dataset, and 2D vs 3D. Our review covered a wide range of articles published between 2010 and 2025, including various methods, datasets, and emerging paradigms. We also reviewed different human body models, loss functions, and evaluation metrics for 2D and 3D HPE. Further- more, we also provide an overview of popular datasets used for HPE tasks and their merits and shortcomings. In addition, we also highlighted several emerging directions in HPE, such as diffusion-based methods, the integration of large language models, and multi-modal approaches. Despite significant advances in HPE, as discussed, there are still challenges that need to be addressed. We have also discussed key challenges in HPE, along with future research directions to address them. We hope that our survey and discussion of promising future research directions serve to inspire researchers to take up these challenges and further advance the field. JSON: Name: diffusion_vlm_biomech_hpe Title: Conditional diffusion-based multi-hypothesis 3D human pose estimation conditioned on vision-language prompts and biomechanical priors for occlusion-robust monocular video Short Hypothesis: Conditioning a diffusion-based multi-hypothesis 3D pose generator on vision-language semantic prompts and explicit biomechanical constraints reduces MPJPE and increases correct-hypothesis recall under occlusion compared with an otherwise identical diffusion baseline without those conditionings. Related Work: Recent multi-hypothesis and generative approaches (diffusion, DDPM/DDIM, conditional VAEs, mixture density networks) address 2D-to-3D depth ambiguity by producing diverse candidate poses but remain computationally expensive and require large sampling at inference. Weakly- and self-supervised lifting methods reduce 3D label dependence but rely on geometric assumptions or multi-view consistency that break under severe occlusion. Transformer and spatio-temporal encoders (MixSTE, TCPFormer, MHFormer) effectively model long-range temporal dependencies but do not explicitly capture multi-modal pose uncertainty nor biomechanical validity. Vision-language and LLM-guided localization frameworks show that language-derived priors can improve keypoint localization, yet they are under-exploited in 3D pose lifting and generally use shallow linear fusion. Biomechanical and kinematic priors (joint-angle limits, constant bone lengths, SCAPE/SMPL constraints) yield anatomically plausible solutions but are rarely integrated into probabilistic generative models at inference. Lightweight and state-space models improve efficiency but sacrifice the multimodal uncertainty modeling needed for occlusion recovery. Overall limitations are: (1) diffusion-based 3D HPE methods lack integrated semantic conditioning and explicit biomechanical priors; (2) VLM/LLM guidance has not been combined with probabilistic multi-hypothesis 3D generators; (3) high computational cost and long inference times prevent real-time use; (4) existing methods show reduced generalization under heavy occlusion, low light, or domain shifts. Abstract: Monocular 3D human pose estimation suffers from depth ambiguity and frequent failures under occlusion. We propose a conditional diffusion framework that generates multiple plausible 3D pose hypotheses per frame and is jointly conditioned on vision-language semantic prompts (automatically extracted from image context and short textual descriptors) and explicit biomechanical priors (joint-angle and inter-joint kinematic constraints). The method integrates temporal pose proxies to preserve motion coherence across video frames and uses an efficient denoising schedule to limit inference cost. Primary contributions are: (1) a conditioning mechanism that fuses language-derived semantic constraints with geometric priors into a diffusion pose generator, (2) an explicit biomechanical constraint module that biases sampling toward anatomically plausible poses, and (3) an evaluation protocol measuring multi-hypothesis correctness, temporal stability, and robustness under occlusion and low-light conditions. We expect the combined conditioning to yield lower MPJPE and higher recall of correct hypotheses under occlusion than diffusion-only baselines, while producing anatomically valid and temporally consistent pose sequences. Experiments: Datasets: train on Human3.6M (controlled 3D), augmented with SURREAL synthetic examples and MPII/COCO 2D in-the-wild images for 2D supervision; evaluate on held-out splits of Human3.6M (in-domain), MPI-INF-3DHP and MuPoTS-3D (in-the-wild / multi-person), EHPT-XC (low-light / motion-blur), and a sports subset (WorldPose or AthletePose3D) for domain generalization. Baselines: (A) diffusion-only multi-hypothesis generator (same backbone, no conditioning), (B) D3DP/DiffPose-style published diffusion method reimplemented to match capacity, (C) MixSTE (deterministic transformer temporal baseline), (D) TCPFormer (state-proxy temporal baseline), (E) RepNet/weakly-supervised triangulation baseline for single-view lifting. Metrics: MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, PCK@0.05/0.1 (normalized), 3D-PCK/3DPCK, AUC, MPJVE (temporal velocity error), multi-hypothesis minMPJPE (lowest MPJPE among k sampled hypotheses), hypothesis recall@τ (fraction of frames where any hypothesis is within τ mm), hypothesis diversity (mean pairwise joint variance), OKS/AP for 2D re-projection, and runtime (ms), FLOPs, and peak memory. Experimental setup: fix input sequence length (e.g., 81 frames) and sample N=20 hypotheses per frame at inference; ablation studies: (1) full model (diffusion + VLM + biomech + temporal proxy), (2) diffusion only, (3) diffusion + biomech priors, (4) diffusion + VLM prompts, (5) diffusion + temporal proxy (no semantic/biomech), (6) number of diffusion steps ablation (e.g., 50, 200, 1000) and sampling strategy ablation (DDIM vs DDPM), (7) varying hypothesis count (5, 10, 20) to measure minMPJPE scaling. Training protocol: identical backbone and parameter budget across comparative ablations; optimizer AdamW, learning rate schedule identical for all; early stopping on validation MPJPE. Statistical analysis: report mean±std over three random seeds; assess significance with paired t-tests (p<0.05) for MPJPE and hypothesis-recall improvements versus baseline (diffusion-only). Cross-dataset generalization: train on Human3.6M+SURREAL, test zero-shot on MPI-INF-3DHP and MuPoTS-3D and report relative MPJPE and recall degradation. Risk Factors and Limitations: High computational cost: diffusion sampling and VLM conditioning increase inference time and memory, potentially preventing real-time operation; scaling to long video sequences or many people may be infeasible on edge devices. VLM/LLM conditioning reliability: automatic semantic prompt extraction may hallucinate or produce inconsistent cues in domain-specific or low-quality images, degrading geometric conditioning. Biomechanical priors mismatch: fixed joint-angle or bone-length priors may not generalize to diverse body shapes, infants, or extreme athletic postures, causing bias or incorrect regularization. Dependence on upstream detectors: errors in initial 2D keypoints or person detection propagate into the diffusion generator, reducing hypothesis quality. Dataset biases: training on lab-collected 3D datasets plus synthetic data risks overfitting to lab-like motions and synthetic appearance; domain shifts (age, body shape, clothing, ethnicity) may reduce generalization. Multi-person grouping and occlusion: sampling multiple hypotheses does not solve instance association in heavy occlusion or severe inter-person overlap and may increase identity switches. Evaluation sensitivity: multi-hypothesis metrics (minMPJPE) favor larger hypothesis counts; improving recall by sampling more hypotheses increases compute and may mask poor single-hypothesis accuracy. Ethical/privacy concerns: VLM conditioning requires image-derived semantic context that may include sensitive information; use in surveillance or healthcare requires nontechnical governance. Finally, integrating language conditioning and biomechanical priors may require careful hyperparameter balancing; poorly tuned weightings can harm both accuracy and plausibility.
